references.text: In [ref:Luk 12:20|Luke 12:20], God calls the rich man a fool because he made plans without considering God—this self-centered planning begins in verse 17, where he deliberates with himself about what to do.
[ref:Ordsp 27:1|Proverbs 27:1] warns against boasting about tomorrow, for no one knows what a day may bring. The rich man’s calculations about the future in Luke 12:17 reflect this arrogant attitude.

[ref:Jak 4:13-16|James 4:13–16] warns against making plans without considering God’s will—"Tomorrow we will go to such and such a city"—which recalls the rich man’s self-centered reflection on how he would gather his crops.

[ref:Fork 2:22-23|Ecclesiastes 2:22–23] asks what advantage a person has from all their toil and planning, which also troubles the mind at night. The rich man’s anxious deliberation about his harvest reflects this emptiness.

[ref:5 Mos 8:17|Deuteronomy 8:17] warns against saying in one’s heart, "My own power and the strength of my own hand have gained me this wealth." The rich man thinks of "my crops" without acknowledging God as the giver.
In [ref:Luk 12:18-19|Luke 12:18–19], the rich man’s inner monologue from verse 17 continues with his decision to tear down his barns and build larger ones—and then live in self-satisfaction.
[ref:Hos 13:15|Hosea 13:15] says that even if someone bears fruit among brothers, an east wind may come and dry up the source. The rich man’s confidence in his crops is just as vulnerable.

[ref:Sal 49:19|Psalm 49:19] describes one who praises themselves while alive but must ultimately leave everything behind. The rich man’s self-centered planning in Luke 12:17 shows exactly this attitude.
